results.message: What did the Punic-speaking people out in the countryside believe?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We cannot tell you. Our whole record comes from two cities, Carthage and Hippo, and from bishops trained to argue in Latin. The countryside, and the language many ordinary people spoke there, which was not the one we were taught in, we do not carry in any detail. We know that Punic and Berber were spoken. We know there were churches in towns and villages between our two cities. What those congregations believed, and how their pastors taught them, in the words they actually spoke -- that is simply not where our own voice was formed.

We can tell you what a bishop taught his own flock, in Latin, in the city. We can tell you that we taught the creed before the water, and that you said it back before we baptized you. We can tell you that Christ's death, burial, and rising were the pattern our own lives were cut to. Cyprian said: “None of us sets himself up as a bishop over other bishops, and none of us uses a tyrant's terror to force a colleague into obedience. Every bishop has his own right to judge, in keeping with the freedom and power allowed to him. He can no more be judged by another bishop than he himself can judge another. Instead, let us all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the only one who has the power both to place us in the government of His Church and to judge how we conduct ourselves there.”

But whether a Punic-speaking congregation in a village church heard those same teachings, in their own tongue, from a pastor whose words do not survive -- we will not invent that to fill the silence.

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258
